title: Partitions are logs
summary: Offsets, segments, time and size retention, log compaction and tombstones: what Kafka actually stores on disk.

steps.title: A topic is a set of append-only logs
body: A Kafka **topic** is split into **partitions**. Each partition is an **append-only log**: the producer adds
records at the end, every record gets the next **offset** (0, 1, 2, ...), and nothing is ever changed in place.
```text
topic "orders" (3 partitions)
P0 | 0 A1:created | 1 C4:created | 2 A1:paid    | 3 A1:shipped |   <- next write: offset 4 (log-end offset)
P1 | 0 B7:created | 1 B7:paid    |                                <- next write: offset 2
P2 | 0 D2:created | 1 E9:created | 2 D2:cancelled |             <- next write: offset 3
billing group reads at 1   analytics group reads at 3
- An offset only means something **inside one partition**: P0 offset 3 and P1 offset 3 are unrelated records.
- **Reading does not remove anything.** Each consumer group keeps its own position (its *committed offset*), so
billing and analytics read the same records independently, and a new group can start from the beginning.
- The **log-end offset** (LEO) is the offset the next record will get. It equals the number of records ever written
to the partition, not the number still stored.
- Records leave the log only through **retention** (old segments are deleted) or **compaction** (older values of a
key are removed). Both come next.
Why a log and not a queue? A log is sequential disk I/O (fast), it allows replay after a bug fix, and many
independent readers cost almost nothing extra.
> **See it:** open **Labs → Messaging builder → Kafka** and play the challenge *Same key, same partition*.

steps.prompt: The billing group has just read and committed `orders` P1 offset 5. What happens to that record?
options: It stays in the log; other groups can still read it, and it leaves only through retention or compaction
It is deleted from P1, like an acknowledged RabbitMQ message
It is moved to a `__consumed` topic
It is hidden from every group until retention removes it
explain: A Kafka consumer only moves **its own group's** position (stored in the internal `__consumer_offsets` topic).
The data stays until the topic's `cleanup.policy` removes it. That is the big difference from a queue: replay and
many readers are free. Nobody on the broker side tracks "who has read what" per record.

steps.title: A partition log
prompt: Model one partition as a log.
Write a class `PartitionLog`:
- `long Append(string? key, string value)`: adds a record at the end and returns its offset (0 for the first record, then 1, 2, ...).
- `long LogEndOffset` (get-only): the offset the next record will get.
- `List<string> Read(long offset, int max)`: returns up to `max` records starting at `offset`, each formatted as
`"{offset}:{key}={value}"` (a `null` key prints as nothing: `"4:=hello"`). Reading at or after the log end returns an
empty list (the consumer simply waits). A negative offset throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
- Reading never removes records.
starter: public long Append(string? key, string value)
public List<string> Read(long offset, int max)
solution: readonly List<(string? Key, string Value)> records = new();
public long Append(string? key, string value)
public List<string> Read(long offset, int max)
for (var o = offset; o < records.Count && result.Count < max; o++)
hints: A `List<(string? Key, string Value)>` is enough: the index is the offset.
`LogEndOffset => records.Count`; `Read` loops from `offset` while `o < records.Count && result.Count < max`.
template: Dojo.Eq("the first record gets offset 0", 0L, dojoLog.Append("A1", "created"));
Dojo.Eq("log-end offset is the next offset to write", 4L, dojoLog.LogEndOffset);
Dojo.Eq("read from the start", new List<string> { "0:A1=created", "1:B7=created" }, dojoLog.Read(0, 2));
Dojo.Eq("read from the middle, null key prints empty", new List<string> { "2:A1=paid", "3:=heartbeat" }, dojoLog.Read(2, 10));
Dojo.Eq("reading does not remove anything", 4, dojoLog.Read(0, 10).Count);
Dojo.Eq("reading at the log end returns nothing yet", new List<string>(), dojoLog.Read(4, 10));

steps.title: Compaction: keep the latest value per key
body: Some topics are not a history but a **table**: the latest address of each customer, the current price of each
product. For those, set `cleanup.policy=compact`:
```text
before compaction                                after compaction (offsets never change)
| 0 cust-1:Leeds | 1 cust-2:York | 2 cust-1:Hull |    | 2 cust-1:Hull | 3 cust-3:Bath | 4 cust-2:null |
| 3 cust-3:Bath  | 4 cust-2:null |
- The log cleaner keeps **at least the last record of every key**. Offsets stay as they were, so the log just has gaps.
- A record with a **null value** is a **tombstone**: "this key is deleted". It is kept for `delete.retention.ms`
(default 1 day) so that slow consumers still see the delete, then it is removed too.
- Only closed segments are cleaned, and only once the dirty share passes `min.cleanable.dirty.ratio` (0.5 by default),
so a compacted topic can still briefly show several values per key. Consumers must handle that.
- Kafka itself uses compaction for `__consumer_offsets` (the latest committed offset per group and partition).
- `cleanup.policy=compact,delete` does both: latest per key, and nothing older than `retention.ms`.
```bash
kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --entity-type topics --entity-name customer-address \
--alter --add-config cleanup.policy=compact,delete.retention.ms=86400000
> **See it:** in **Labs → Messaging builder → Kafka**, play *Latest value per key*.

items: `orders` events: created, paid, shipped, kept 7 days
`customer-address`: the current address of every customer
`__consumer_offsets`: the latest committed offset per group and partition
`product-price`: the current price per SKU, read on start-up to warm a cache
`audit-log` that must keep every change for 90 days
explain: Compaction suits topics where only the **current state per key** matters and a new reader should be able to
rebuild that state. Event histories, click streams and audits need every record: delete-by-retention.

steps.title: Compact a log
prompt: Write `List<Rec> Compact(List<Rec> log, long nowMs, long deleteRetentionMs)` that does what the log cleaner does
(simplified: the whole log is cleanable).
The record type is given (do not declare it): `record Rec(long Offset, string Key, string? Value, long TimestampMs);`
- keep only the **last** record of each key (the one with the highest offset), with its original offset;
- keep the result in offset order;
- a tombstone (`Value == null`) that is the last record of its key is kept **unless** it is old enough:
remove it when `nowMs - TimestampMs >= deleteRetentionMs`.
starter: List<Rec> Compact(List<Rec> log, long nowMs, long deleteRetentionMs)
solution: List<Rec> Compact(List<Rec> log, long nowMs, long deleteRetentionMs)
foreach (var r in log) last[r.Key] = r.Offset;
.Where(r => r.Value is not null || nowMs - r.TimestampMs < deleteRetentionMs)
hints: First pass: a `Dictionary<string, long>` from key to its highest offset.
Second pass: keep `r` when `last[r.Key] == r.Offset`, then drop tombstones whose age is `>= deleteRetentionMs`.
template: Dojo.Eq("latest value per key, offsets kept, fresh tombstone kept",
new List<Rec> { new(2, "cust-1", "addr=Hull", 3000), new(3, "cust-3", "addr=Bath", 4000), new(4, "cust-2", null, 5000) },
Dojo.Eq("an old tombstone is finally removed",
Dojo.Eq("a key written again after its tombstone comes back",
Dojo.Eq("an empty log stays empty", new List<Rec>(), Compact(new List<Rec>(), 0, 1));
record Rec(long Offset, string Key, string? Value, long TimestampMs);

steps.title: Segments and retention
body: On disk a partition is a folder of **segment** files, named after their first offset:
```text
/var/lib/kafka/data/orders-0/
00000000000000000000.log   .index  .timeindex    closed segment: offsets 0..41876
00000000000000041877.log   .index  .timeindex    closed segment: offsets 41877..83990
00000000000000083991.log   .index  .timeindex    ACTIVE segment: new records go here
- The active segment **rolls** (closes, a new one starts) when it reaches `segment.bytes` (1 GiB default) or is
older than `segment.ms` (7 days default).
- **Retention deletes whole closed segments**, oldest first, never the active one. A segment goes when its
**newest** record is older than `retention.ms` (default 604800000 = 7 days), or while the partition is bigger than
`retention.bytes` (default -1 = no size limit, and it is **per partition**, not per topic).
- So a record can live longer than `retention.ms`: it waits until its whole segment is old. A quiet topic with a big
`segment.bytes` may keep data for weeks.
- When segments go, the **log start offset** moves forward. A consumer whose committed offset is now below it gets
`OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE`, and `auto.offset.reset` decides where it restarts (the records in between are simply gone).
```bash
kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --entity-type topics --entity-name orders \
--alter --add-config retention.ms=1209600000      # 14 days for this topic only
kafka-get-offsets.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --topic orders --time -2   # log start offset per partition
> **See it:** in **Labs → Messaging builder → Kafka**, play *Retention ate the backlog*.

steps.prompt: Retention runs at hour 180 with `retention.ms` set to 168 hours. Each tuple is a segment's base offset and the hour of its newest record; the last segment is the active one. What does this print?
code: var segments = new[] { (Base: 0L, Newest: 10), (Base: 1000L, Newest: 50), (Base: 2000L, Newest: 170), (Base: 3000L, Newest: 175) };
explain: Only the first segment is entirely older than 168 hours (its newest record is 170 hours old), so it is deleted and
the log now starts at offset 1000. The second segment holds records from hour 50 and earlier, which is 130 hours ago:
kept. Retention works on whole segments, oldest first, and stops at the first one it must keep.

steps.title: Segments and retention
prompt: Grow the log into what a broker really keeps: segments and time retention.
Write a class `SegmentedLog`:
- `SegmentedLog(int segmentSize)`: a segment holds at most `segmentSize` records. When the last (active) segment is
full, the **next** append starts a new segment.
- `long Append(string value, long timestampMs)`: appends and returns the offset (0, 1, 2, ...).
- `long LogStartOffset`: the offset of the oldest record still stored (the log-end offset when nothing was written).
- `long LogEndOffset`: the next offset to write.
- `int SegmentCount`.
- `int EnforceRetention(long nowMs, long retentionMs)`: deletes closed segments from the oldest while their **newest**
record is older than retention (`nowMs - newestTimestamp > retentionMs`); stops at the first one that must stay;
never deletes the active (last) segment. Returns how many segments it deleted.
- `List<string> Read(long offset, int max)`: up to `max` records from `offset` as `"{offset}:{value}"`. An offset
below `LogStartOffset` or above `LogEndOffset` throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` (Kafka's `OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE`);
reading exactly at `LogEndOffset` returns an empty list.
starter: public long Append(string value, long timestampMs) => 0;
public int EnforceRetention(long nowMs, long retentionMs) => 0;
public List<string> Read(long offset, int max) => new();
solution: readonly List<List<(long Offset, string Value, long Ts)>> segments = new() { new() };
public long LogStartOffset => segments[0].Count > 0 ? segments[0][0].Offset : next;
public long Append(string value, long timestampMs)
public int EnforceRetention(long nowMs, long retentionMs)
public List<string> Read(long offset, int max)
hints: Keep a `List<List<...>>` of segments, starting with one empty segment; the last one is the active segment.
`Append`: if `segments[^1].Count == segmentSize`, add a new segment first.
Retention: `while (segments.Count > 1 && nowMs - segments[0][^1].Ts > retentionMs)` remove the first segment.
template: Dojo.Eq("first retention pass deletes only the expired segment", 1, dojoS.EnforceRetention(6500, 4000));
Dojo.Eq("log start offset moved to 2", 2L, dojoS.LogStartOffset);
Dojo.Eq("log end offset did not move", 5L, dojoS.LogEndOffset);
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>("a committed offset below the log start is out of range", () => dojoS.Read(0, 10));
Dojo.Eq("reading from the log start", new List<string> { "2:c", "3:d", "4:e" }, dojoS.Read(2, 10));
Dojo.Eq("reading at the log end is empty", new List<string>(), dojoS.Read(5, 10));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>("beyond the log end is out of range", () => dojoS.Read(6, 1));
Dojo.Eq("much later: the active segment survives even when old", 1, dojoS.EnforceRetention(100000, 4000));
Dojo.Eq("only the active segment is left", 1, dojoS.SegmentCount);
Dojo.Eq("the active segment still has room", 5L, dojoS.Append("f", 100001));
Dojo.Eq("a full active segment rolls on the next append", 6L, dojoS.Append("g", 100002));
